Machu Picchu lies about 75 km to the north-west.
Q5582862.w: A city of red-brown roofs filling a high, narrow valley; bare mountains around; a runway squeezed along the valley floor.
f: Tradition says the Inca city was laid out in the shape of a puma.
The historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983.
The snowy peak of Ausangate, over 6,300 m high, rises about 100 km to the south-east.

q.q: Which empire had its capital at Cuzco?

Q272795.t: A green oasis at Peru's southern tip
Q272795.s: Tacna is a patch of green in one of the driest places on Earth, the northern edge of the Atacama Desert, where rain may add up to only a few millimetres a year. The city lives off the thin Caplina River coming down from the Andes, whose snowy peaks line the eastern horizon. The border with Chile runs only about 35 km to the south.
Q272795.w: A mid-sized city in otherwise bare, beige desert; green irrigated fields along a narrow valley; the Andes rising to the east.
f: Tacna is the southernmost city in Peru.
Olive groves around the city make the region one of Peru's main olive producers.

q.q: Which country's border lies just south of Tacna?

Q214173.t: An oval colonial core beside a vast mud-brick ruin
Q214173.s: Trujillo sits on the desert coast of northern Peru, its old centre neatly enclosed by an oval avenue that follows the line of the colonial city wall. Just west, towards the sea, sprawl the eroded mud-brick ruins of Chan Chan, capital of the Chimú kingdom and the largest adobe city of the pre-Columbian Americas. The Spanish founded Trujillo in 1534.
Q214173.w: A city on a desert coastal plain between the sea and bare mountains; green irrigated valley fields around it.
f: Chan Chan's ruins cover about 20 km² and have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1986.
The city is named after Trujillo in Spain, home town of Francisco Pizarro.
Fishermen at nearby Huanchaco still head out on small reed boats called caballitos de totora.

q.q: Which people built Chan Chan, near Trujillo?

Q840712.t: Vineyards and giant dunes in the Peruvian desert
Q840712.s: Ica is a green oasis in the coastal desert of southern Peru, watered by a river from the Andes and surrounded by huge sand dunes. Its irrigated valley is the heart of Peru's grape growing and the home of pisco, the local grape brandy. Just west of the city, the tiny lagoon of Huacachina sits in a hollow ringed by towering dunes.
Q840712.w: A city in a green valley strip cutting through pale desert; big, sharp-crested dunes to the west.
f: The famous Nazca Lines lie roughly 100 km to the south-east, though they are too fine to see from cruise height.
Rain is so rare here that the valley depends almost entirely on water from the Andes.

q.q: What is Huacachina, near Ica?

Q2933.t: The 'Mother of Cities' on a bend of the Paraguay River
Q2933.s: Asunción spreads along the east bank of the Paraguay River where it curves around a wide bay. Across the water begins the Chaco, a flat, green-brown plain of marshes and scrub running west for hundreds of kilometres. Founded in 1537, it is one of the oldest cities in South America, and its settlers went on to found many others, including Buenos Aires for good in 1580.
Q2933.w: A city on the outside of a big river bend, beside a rounded bay; flat, wet, scrubby plains across the river to the west.
f: The Pilcomayo River joins the Paraguay just downstream of the city.
Santa Cruz de la Sierra, now in Bolivia, was also founded by an expedition from Asunción, in 1561.

q.q: Why is Asunción called the 'Mother of Cities'?
q.a: Its settlers founded many other cities
x: It is the oldest city in the Americas

Q3274.t: A lakeside capital dotted with round crater lakes
Q3274.s: Managua stretches along the southern shore of Lake Managua, and within the city itself you can spot small, round crater lakes — old volcanic vents now filled with water. At the far north-western end of the lake rises the near-perfect cone of Momotombo. The city became Nicaragua's capital in 1852, a compromise between the rival cities of León and Granada.
Q3274.w: A low, sprawling city on a big lake's south shore; round blue crater lakes in and around it; a volcanic cone to the north-west.
f: Laguna de Asososca, one of the crater lakes, supplies part of the city's drinking water.
Lake Nicaragua, the largest lake in Central America, lies about 30 km to the south-east.

q.q: Why was Managua made Nicaragua's capital in 1852?
q.a: As a compromise between rival cities

Q3306.t: Where ships queue for the Panama Canal
Q3306.s: Look out to sea off Panama City and you'll often see dozens of ships at anchor, waiting their turn for the canal. The city's towers line a curving bay right beside the canal's Pacific entrance. Founded in 1519, the original town was the first European city on the Pacific coast of the Americas. The canal itself opened in 1914 and cuts about 80 km across the isthmus.
Q3306.w: A high-rise city along a curving bay; ships dotted offshore; a canal channel and a bridge just west of the city.
f: Oddly, the canal's Pacific end lies further east than its Atlantic end.
The Amador Causeway, linking small islands at the canal mouth, was built with rock dug out for the canal.
Locks lift ships about 26 m to Gatún Lake in the middle of the isthmus.

q.q: Which end of the Panama Canal lies further east?
x: Both lie on the same longitude

Q124739.t: A city pressed right up against the US border
Q124739.s: Tijuana fills a jumble of mesas and canyons in Mexico's far north-west corner, and its northern edge is a hard, straight line: the border with the United States, with San Diego beyond. The airport's runway runs just south of that line, so close that a footbridge lets passengers walk straight in from the US side. The city was officially founded in 1889.
Q124739.w: A dense city on hilly, canyon-cut ground, cut off to the north by a sharp straight line; the Pacific to the west.
f: The San Ysidro crossing between Tijuana and San Diego is one of the busiest land border crossings in the world.
The Tijuana River flows north across the border and reaches the Pacific in the US.

q.q: What runs right alongside Tijuana airport's runway?

Q61302.t: A high-desert capital, gateway to the Copper Canyon
Q61302.s: Chihuahua sits on a wide, dry plateau about 1,400 m up, ringed by bare, rocky ranges; it is the capital of Mexico's largest state. It was founded in 1709 as a silver-mining town. From here the Chihuahua–Pacific railway heads south-west across the Sierra Madre and through the Copper Canyon, a system of gorges that is deeper in places than the Grand Canyon.
Q61302.w: A city on a flat, tan high-desert basin, encircled by bare rocky ranges; the dark Sierra Madre far to the west.
f: The Chihuahua–Pacific railway, completed in 1961, crosses dozens of bridges and runs through dozens of tunnels.
The tiny dog breed takes its name from the state of Chihuahua.

q.q: What sets out from Chihuahua through the Copper Canyon?
q.a: A railway to the Pacific coast

Q40194.t: A Pacific port on a peninsula, just south of the tropic
Q40194.s: Mazatlán sits on a rocky peninsula on Mexico's Pacific coast, with a long seafront curving north along the beach and three small islands just offshore. The Tropic of Cancer passes only about 25 km to the north, so at the June solstice the midday sun here is almost directly overhead. The name comes from Nahuatl and means 'place of deer'.
Q40194.w: A city on a knobbly peninsula and along a long, straight beach; small islands offshore; green hills and the Sierra Madre inland.
f: The lighthouse on Cerro del Crestón shines from about 157 m above the sea, one of the highest in the world.
Ferries cross the Gulf of California from here to La Paz, in Baja California.

q.q: What does 'Mazatlán' mean in Nahuatl?

Q273014.t: An oil port among lagoons at the mouth of the Pánuco
Q273014.s: Tampico lies a few kilometres up the Pánuco River from the Gulf of Mexico, and water is everywhere: lagoons within the city, marshes around it, the wide brown river on its southern side. In the early 1900s oil struck nearby turned it into one of the busiest oil ports in the world. Look for the long cable-stayed bridge across the river.
Q273014.w: A city between lagoons and a wide river near the coast; marshes all around; a long bridge across the river to the south.
f: The modern city was refounded in 1823 near the site of an older colonial settlement.
Laguna del Carpintero, a lagoon right in the city, is home to crocodiles.

q.q: What made Tampico boom in the early 1900s?

Q81398.t: A horseshoe bay ringed by a hillside amphitheatre
Q81398.s: Acapulco wraps around one of the most perfectly shaped bays on the Pacific, a deep blue horseshoe with the city climbing the steep hills on all sides like the seats of an amphitheatre. For some 250 years, from 1565, Spanish galleons sailed from here to Manila, carrying silver west and bringing back silk and porcelain from Asia.
Q81398.w: A deep, rounded bay almost closed by headlands; white buildings climbing the green hills around it; long beaches to the east.
f: Cliff divers at La Quebrada plunge about 35 m into a narrow rocky inlet.
The star-shaped Fort of San Diego was built in the 1600s to guard the galleon harbour.

q.q: Which Asian port did Acapulco's galleons sail to?

Q173270.t: Where Cortés came ashore, with Orizaba on the horizon
Q173270.s: Veracruz lies on a low, sandy stretch of the Gulf of Mexico coast, with a busy port and, offshore, the pale shapes of coral reefs in turquoise water. Hernán Cortés landed on this coast in 1519 and founded Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, the first Spanish town in what is now Mexico. On clear days, look west for the white cone of Pico de Orizaba.
Q173270.w: A flat port city on a straight Gulf coast; breakwaters and docks; pale reef patches offshore; a snowy volcano far inland to the west.
f: The fortress of San Juan de Ulúa, begun in the 1500s, stands on a former island at the harbour mouth.
The reefs off the city are protected as a national marine park.
The town's site shifted more than once before it settled here around 1600.

q.q: What does the name Veracruz mean?

Q207429.t: A valley city on the edge of a 1,000-metre canyon
Q207429.s: Tuxtla Gutiérrez spreads across a warm, green valley in Chiapas, and just to its north-east the land splits open: the Sumidero Canyon, where the Grijalva River runs between cliffs rising up to about 1,000 m. From above it looks like a dark crack in the plateau. The name Tuxtla comes from a Nahuatl word usually translated as 'place of rabbits'.
Q207429.w: A long city in an east–west valley; to the north-east, a deep, winding gorge with a green-blue river at the bottom.
f: Downstream, the Chicoasén Dam turns the river into a long reservoir winding through the mountains.
The second half of the name honours Joaquín Miguel Gutiérrez, a 19th-century politician from Chiapas.

q.q: Which canyon lies just north-east of Tuxtla Gutiérrez?

Q8969.t: A resort shaped like a 7 on turquoise water
Q8969.s: Cancún's hotel zone is easy to spot: a thin strip of white sand shaped like the number 7, with the turquoise Caribbean on one side and the calm, darker Nichupté Lagoon on the other. Until about 1970 there was almost nothing here; the resort was planned from scratch. Inland stretches the flat green Yucatán, without a single river on its surface.
Q8969.w: A narrow white island shaped like a 7 enclosing a lagoon; bright turquoise sea to the east; flat green jungle inland.
f: Just offshore begins the Mesoamerican Reef, the second-largest barrier reef system in the world.
On the Yucatán's limestone, rainwater drains underground into sinkholes called cenotes.
Isla Mujeres, a small island to the north, lies about 13 km across the water.

q.q: What shape is the island of Cancún's hotel zone?

Q165204.t: The White City above a buried asteroid crater
Q165204.s: Mérida spreads over the dead-flat limestone plain of the Yucatán, with no river, hill or lake to break the scrub. Beneath it lies a secret: the buried Chicxulub crater, blasted by the asteroid that helped end the age of dinosaurs, is centred on the coast just north of the city. The Spanish founded Mérida in 1542 on the site of the Maya city of T'hó.
Q165204.w: A large, low, pale city on a perfectly flat green plain; the coast and the port of Progreso about 35 km to the north.
f: A ring of cenotes, water-filled sinkholes, traces part of the crater's buried rim around the city.
In the late 1800s sisal fibre from henequen plantations made Mérida one of Mexico's richest cities.
The crater is about 180 km across, but it lies buried and cannot be seen from the air.

q.q: What lies buried beneath the land around Mérida?

Q2900.t: A long, thin capital on a volcano, just below the equator
Q2900.s: Quito is squeezed into a narrow Andean valley about 2,850 m up, stretching some 40 km from north to south along the flank of the Pichincha volcano. The equator runs only about 25 km to the north. On a clear day, look south for the perfect snow cone of Cotopaxi. In 1978 Quito's old town was among the very first places named a World Heritage site.
Q2900.w: A long, narrow city pressed against the slopes of a large volcano; deep ravines to the east; snowy cones on the horizon.
f: Cotopaxi, about 5,900 m high, is one of the highest active volcanoes in the world.
The airport stands on a plateau east of the city, lower than Quito itself.

q.q: How far is Quito from the equator?

Q3070.t: A capital in a green valley ringed by volcanoes
Q3070.s: San José fills the heart of Costa Rica's Central Valley, about 1,150 m up: a bowl of red roofs and coffee-green hills rimmed by volcanoes. To the north rise Poás and Barva, to the east Irazú and Turrialba. From Irazú's summit, on a rare clear day, both the Pacific and the Caribbean are visible. The city became the national capital in 1823.
Q3070.w: A sprawling city filling a green valley, with volcanic mountains to the north and east; coffee plantations on the slopes.
f: Irazú, about 3,430 m high, is Costa Rica's highest volcano.
Coffee grown on the volcanic slopes in the 1800s paid for much of the city's early grandeur, including its National Theatre.

q.q: From which volcano near San José can both oceans be seen?

Q3110.t: A capital between a volcano and a caldera lake
Q3110.s: San Salvador spreads across a valley at the foot of the San Salvador volcano, whose summit crater, El Boquerón, is a gaping round pit about 1.5 km wide. East of the city lies Lake Ilopango, filling the caldera of a colossal eruption some 1,500 years ago. Spanish settlers moved the town to this valley in the 1500s, and today it is the nation's capital.
Q3110.w: A dense city at the eastern foot of a big volcano with a round summit crater; a large blue caldera lake to the east.
f: The Boquerón crater is roughly 500 m deep, with a small cone inside it.
Lake Ilopango covers about 70 km².

q.q: Which lake fills the caldera east of San Salvador?

Q34692.t: A harbour city behind a long, thin sand spit
Q34692.s: Kingston faces one of the world's great natural harbours, sealed off from the Caribbean by the Palisadoes, a sand spit more than 10 km long and barely wide enough for a road and the airport runway. At its tip lies Port Royal, once a notorious haunt of buccaneers. Behind the city rise the Blue Mountains, home of one of the world's most famous coffees.
Q34692.w: A wide, calm harbour enclosed by a long, curving spit with a runway; a sprawling city below mountains to the north.
f: Blue Mountain Peak, about 2,260 m high, is the highest point in Jamaica.
Kingston was laid out in 1692 and became Jamaica's capital in 1872.

q.q: What sits on the long spit enclosing Kingston Harbour?

Q657461.t: A walled colonial port among bays and lagoons
Q657461.s: Cartagena is a maze of water: a large, sheltered bay with islands, inner lagoons and channels, and a narrow peninsula lined with white towers. At its heart the old town is still ringed by colonial stone walls, about 11 km of them, built to protect a treasure port. Pedro de Heredia founded the city in 1533; its walled centre is a World Heritage site.
Q657461.w: A coastal city spread around bays and lagoons; a thin peninsula of high-rises; islands in the bay; coral islets to the south-west.
f: The Rosario Islands, a coral archipelago south-west of the city, are protected as a national park.
Spanish treasure fleets called here to load silver and gold bound for Spain.

q.q: What surrounds Cartagena's old town?

Q130242.t: A river town lost in an ocean of Amazon forest
Q130242.s: Mitú is a small town on the Vaupés River in Colombia's far south-east, surrounded in every direction by unbroken rainforest. No road connects it with the rest of the country; people and goods arrive by plane or by boat. From above, the river winds through the green like a dark ribbon, with the town's clearing and airstrip on its bank.
Q130242.w: A small clearing with an airstrip beside a winding dark river; endless green forest canopy all around.
f: The Vaupés flows east into Brazil, where, as the Uaupés, it joins the Rio Negro.
Most of the region's inhabitants belong to indigenous peoples such as the Cubeo and Tukano.

q.q: How do you reach Mitú from the rest of Colombia?
q.a: Only by air or by river

Q1555.t: A ravine-cut plateau capital watched by volcanoes
Q1555.s: Guatemala City sits on a highland plateau about 1,500 m up, and deep green ravines cut into it, so the city spreads along flat fingers of land between them. To the south-west stands a row of volcanoes: Agua, Acatenango and Fuego, which often trails a plume of ash. The capital moved here in 1776 from Antigua, in the next valley to the west.
Q1555.w: A large city on a plateau split by deep green ravines; tall volcanic cones to the south-west, one often smoking.
f: The ruins of Kaminaljuyú, a large Maya settlement founded more than 2,000 years ago, lie within today's city.
Pacaya, another active volcano, rises just south of the city.

q.q: Which city was Guatemala's capital before 1776?

Q44401.t: A slice of France on the edge of the Amazon forest
Q44401.s: Cayenne sits on a small, hilly peninsula at the mouth of the Cayenne River, with muddy brown sea in front and rainforest behind. French Guiana is part of France, so this is a European Union city in South America, and it uses the euro. About 60 km up the coast lies Kourou, where Europe's rockets are launched close to the equator.
Q44401.w: A small city on a knobbly peninsula at a river mouth; brown, muddy sea; dense green forest inland.
f: The brown coastal water is stained by Amazon silt, carried north-west along the shore by currents.
Forest covers the vast majority of French Guiana's land.

q.q: Which currency is used in Cayenne?

Q51599.t: A windswept port on the Strait of Magellan
Q51599.s: Punta Arenas stretches along the western shore of the Strait of Magellan, facing the low, tawny hills of Tierra del Fuego across the water. Ferdinand Magellan's ships threaded this passage in 1520. Before the Panama Canal opened, the town was a busy coaling stop for steamers passing between the oceans. Today planes leave from here for Antarctica.
Q51599.w: A city strung along a wide grey-blue strait; open, treeless steppe inland; the flat shores of Tierra del Fuego across the water.
f: Chile founded the city in 1848.
It is one of the southernmost cities in the world with more than 100,000 people.

q.q: Which strait does Punta Arenas face?

Q14440.t: A desert port wedged under a cliff and a giant dune
Q14440.s: Iquique occupies a narrow ledge between the Pacific and a coastal escarpment that rises some 600 m straight behind it — the edge of the Atacama Desert. Inside the city sits a huge sand dune, Cerro Dragón. Up on the bare plateau inland lie the ghost towns of the 19th-century nitrate boom that made this port rich.
Q14440.w: A city on a thin coastal strip under a tall tan escarpment; a large pale dune among the houses; utterly bare desert above.
f: The abandoned Humberstone and Santa Laura nitrate works inland are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Rain is so rare here that years can pass without a single shower.

q.q: What unusual natural feature stands inside Iquique?

Q3612.t: A copper port on a desert coast by the tropic
Q3612.s: Antofagasta stretches for kilometres along a narrow strip of coast, hemmed in by the bare brown wall of the Coastal Range and the cold blue Pacific. The Tropic of Capricorn crosses just north of the city. Inland lies some of the driest land on Earth, and some of the world's biggest copper mines, whose metal is shipped out through this port.
Q3612.w: A long, thin city along a straight coast beneath a steep brown escarpment; completely bare desert beyond.
f: The desert skies are so clear that major observatories, including Paranal, stand about 120 km to the south.
The city was founded in 1868 to serve mining in the desert.
La Portada, a natural sea arch just north of the city, is a protected natural monument.

q.q: Which line of latitude passes just north of Antofagasta?

Q33986.t: A port city climbing dozens of hills round a bay
Q33986.s: Valparaíso wraps around a wide bay in a steep amphitheatre, its houses climbing more than forty hills that rise straight from a thin strip of flat land by the port. For decades before the Panama Canal it was the main stop for ships rounding Cape Horn. Its maze of hillside neighbourhoods is a World Heritage site, and Viña del Mar merges with it to the north.
Q33986.w: A crescent bay with a port; the city rising steeply up many hills behind it; a resort city continuing along the coast to the north.
f: Some of the funicular lifts that carry people up the hills date from the late 1800s.
Santiago lies about 110 km to the south-east, beyond the Coastal Range.

q.q: How do many people in Valparaíso ride up the hills?

Q160687.t: A city of rivers in Chile's green, rainy south
Q160687.s: Valdivia is laced with water: several rivers meet here and wind west through wetlands and forest to the sea at Corral Bay, about 15 km away. Around it grows dense, evergreen temperate rainforest, fed by heavy rain. Pedro de Valdivia founded the city in 1552 and named it after himself. From the 1850s German settlers arrived and left their mark on the town.
Q160687.w: A city on meandering dark rivers amid green wetlands and forest; the rivers widening west into a bay on the Pacific.
f: In the 1600s and 1700s the Spanish ringed Corral Bay with forts to guard the river route to the city.
Sea lions often lounge beside the riverside fish market in the city centre.

q.q: Who is Valdivia named after?

Q1880.t: A university city at the mouth of the broad Biobío
Q1880.s: Concepción sits where the Biobío, one of Chile's longest and widest rivers, spreads out before reaching the Pacific, crossed here by several long bridges. Lagoons dot the city, and the port of Talcahuano lies on the bay just to the north. For centuries the Biobío marked the frontier between Spanish Chile and the lands of the Mapuche.
Q1880.w: A city between low hills and a very wide river mouth crossed by long bridges; a large bay with a port to the north.
f: In the mid-1700s the city moved to its present site from the nearby coast at Penco.
The Universidad de Concepción, founded in 1919, is one of Chile's oldest universities.

q.q: Which river reaches the sea at Concepción?

Q36214.t: Where Chile's mainland breaks into fjords and islands
Q36214.s: Puerto Montt marks the point where Chile's long Central Valley meets the sea and the coast begins to shatter into fjords, channels and islands. The city sits on the Reloncaví Sound, with Chiloé Island to the south-west and, to the north-east, the snowy, near-perfect cone of Osorno volcano rising beyond Lake Llanquihue. German settlers founded it in 1853.
Q36214.w: A city on a sheltered sound full of islands; a big lake just to the north; snow-capped volcanic cones to the north-east.
f: The Carretera Austral, a road of more than 1,200 km into Patagonia, begins here.
Lake Llanquihue, just north of the city, covers about 860 km².

q.q: Which famous road begins at Puerto Montt?

Q226.t: A small Arctic capital at the mouth of a giant fjord
Q226.s: Nuuk clings to a rocky headland at the mouth of a vast fjord system that reaches more than 100 km inland towards the Greenland ice sheet. Across the water rises the sharp peak of Sermitsiaq. The name simply means 'headland'. The missionary Hans Egede founded the colony here in 1728, but Norse farmers had lived in these fjords centuries earlier.
Q226.w: A small town on a bare rocky peninsula between fjord arms; dark peaks and icebergs around; the white ice sheet far inland.
f: Norse settlers farmed the fjords near Nuuk from about the year 1000 until the mid-1300s.
Nuuk is one of the northernmost capitals in the world.
Sermitsiaq, the landmark peak across the fjord, rises about 1,200 m straight from the sea.

q.q: What does the name Nuuk mean?

Q941136.t: A far-west Amazon town on a wildly winding river
Q941136.s: Cruzeiro do Sul lies near Brazil's western edge, on the Juruá River, one of the most tightly meandering rivers on Earth. From above, the Juruá loops back on itself again and again, leaving crescent-shaped oxbow lakes in the forest. To the west, the low green hills of the Serra do Divisor rise towards the border with Peru. The name means 'Southern Cross'.
Q941136.w: A small town on a river looping in tight curves through unbroken forest; crescent lakes left by old bends; hills to the west.
f: The westernmost point of Brazil lies in the Serra do Divisor, west of the town.
It is the second-largest town in the state of Acre.

q.q: What is Cruzeiro do Sul named after?

Q214913.t: Where three countries meet on the Amazon
Q214913.s: Leticia sits on the north bank of the Amazon at the point where Colombia, Brazil and Peru meet. The town runs straight into Brazil's Tabatinga, with only a street marking the border, while Peru lies across the wide, island-studded river. No road reaches it from the rest of Colombia; the Amazon and the airport are its lifelines.
Q214913.w: Twin towns on the bank of a very wide brown river with long forested islands; endless forest on every side.
f: Thanks to Leticia, Colombia holds a stretch of Amazon riverbank about 100 km long.
The town was founded in 1867.

q.q: Which Brazilian town is joined to Leticia?

Q40236.t: Where black water and brown water flow side by side
Q40236.s: Just below Manaus, look for one of the great sights of the Amazon: the Meeting of the Waters. The dark, tea-coloured Rio Negro meets the pale, muddy Solimões, and for several kilometres the two run side by side in one channel without mixing. The city itself, deep in the rainforest, grew rich in the rubber boom of the late 1800s.
Q40236.w: A big city on the north bank of a dark river; downstream, a sharp line where black and coffee-coloured water meet.
f: The waters stay apart because they differ in temperature, speed and the silt they carry.
Ocean-going ships sail some 1,500 km up the Amazon to reach the city's port.
The Teatro Amazonas opera house, opened in 1896, was built with rubber-boom wealth.

q.q: Which two rivers form the Meeting of the Waters at Manaus?
q.a: The Rio Negro and the Solimões

Q997107.t: A river town among babassu palms in Maranhão
Q997107.s: Caxias lies on the Itapecuru River in the interior of Maranhão, where the dry cerrado savanna gives way to the wetter forests of the Amazon basin. The country around it is dotted with babassu palms, whose oily nuts are gathered by hand. The poet Gonçalves Dias, author of 'Song of Exile', one of Brazil's best-loved poems, was born near here in 1823.
Q997107.w: A mid-sized town on a winding river in rolling green country; scattered palm groves and patches of savanna.
f: Brazil's famous military leader, the Duke of Caxias, took his noble title from this town.
The Itapecuru River flows north to the Atlantic near São Luís.

q.q: Which famous Brazilian poet was born near Caxias?

Q659450.t: Where the blue Tapajós meets the muddy Amazon
Q659450.s: Santarém sits right on a colour line: the clear, blue-green Tapajós flows into the brown, silt-laden Amazon in front of the city, and the two waters run side by side for kilometres. Upstream the Tapajós widens into a lake-like reach fringed with white sand beaches. Jesuits founded a mission here in 1661, roughly halfway between Manaus and Belém.
Q659450.w: A town on a point between a blue-green river and a much wider brown one; pale sandbanks and forest around.
f: In 1928 Henry Ford built a rubber-plantation town, Fordlândia, far up the Tapajós.
In the dry season the falling Tapajós uncovers white beaches at nearby Alter do Chão.

q.q: Which river meets the Amazon at Santarém?

Q509818.t: A frontier city where two Amazon rivers meet
Q509818.s: Marabá sits on a point of land where the Itacaiúnas River flows into the broad Tocantins, in the south-east of Pará. The town grew in the early 1900s on the Brazil-nut trade. Look around it for the patchwork of pasture and remnant forest. To the west lie the hills of Carajás, home to one of the world's largest iron-ore mines.
Q509818.w: A city on a point where two broad rivers meet; flooded islands and sandbars; pastures and forest patches all around.
f: The Carajás Railway, carrying iron ore about 900 km to the coast near São Luís, crosses the Tocantins here.
In the rainy season the rivers rise several metres and often flood the low parts of town.

q.q: Which huge iron-ore district lies west of Marabá?

Q1749958.t: A plateau town at the gateway to Rondônia
Q1749958.s: Vilhena sits on the broad Parecis plateau, about 600 m up, at the south-eastern entrance to the state of Rondônia. From above, the land around it is ruled into vast rectangles of soy and maize, with strips of forest along the streams. The town began as a station on the telegraph line that Cândido Rondon's expeditions pushed into the Amazon in the early 1900s.
Q1749958.w: A town on a flat plateau among huge rectangular fields; a highway running straight through; forest strips along the streams.
f: It is named after Álvaro Vilhena, a director of Brazil's telegraph service.
The BR-364 highway through town is the main road link between Rondônia and the rest of Brazil.

q.q: What did Vilhena begin as?

Q983815.t: A river town amid Rondônia's fishbone clearings
Q983815.s: Ji-Paraná straddles the Machado River, also called the Ji-Paraná, in the heart of Rondônia. Around it lies one of the most striking patterns on the planet: long, straight side roads branching off the main highway, each lined with clearings, so the forest looks cut into a giant fishbone. Most of this settlement dates from the 1970s onward.
Q983815.w: A city on both banks of a winding river; a ladder-like pattern of fields and roads cut into the surrounding forest.
f: It is the second-largest city in Rondônia, after the capital, Porto Velho.
The river flows north to join the Madeira, one of the Amazon's great tributaries.

q.q: What pattern do forest clearings form around Ji-Paraná?

Q168929.t: The 'Brown City' on red soil, gateway to the Pantanal
Q168929.s: Campo Grande spreads across a gentle plateau in Brazil's centre-west, laid out with broad, tree-lined avenues. The soil here is a deep reddish-brown, which earned it the nickname Cidade Morena, the 'Brown City'. Around it lie cattle pastures and soy fields, and a couple of hundred kilometres west begins the Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland.
Q168929.w: A spacious city on a gently rolling plateau; red-brown soil showing between the fields and pastures all around.
f: Sobá, a noodle soup brought by immigrants from Okinawa, is an official part of the city's cultural heritage.
The city became capital of the new state of Mato Grosso do Sul, created in 1977.

q.q: What is Campo Grande's nickname, inspired by its soil?

Q132997.t: An island capital of lagoons, dunes and beaches
Q132997.s: Most of Florianópolis lies on Santa Catarina Island, a green, hilly island about 50 km long, joined to the mainland by bridges. Look for the Lagoa da Conceição, a long lagoon behind white dunes, and dozens of beaches strung along the coast. Settlers from the Azores arrived in the 1700s, and the city took its present name in 1894.
Q132997.w: A long, hilly island parallel to the coast, with a lagoon and pale dunes on its east side; bridges to the mainland.
f: The Hercílio Luz Bridge, opened in 1926, is Brazil's longest suspension bridge.
The name honours Floriano Peixoto, one of the first presidents of the Brazilian republic.

q.q: Where does most of Florianópolis lie?

Q194343.t: A crossroads city that grew from a cattle fair
Q194343.s: Feira de Santana sits on a gentle plateau about 100 km inland from Salvador, where Bahia's green coastal belt starts giving way to the dry sertão. The town grew in the 1700s around a cattle fair beside a chapel of Saint Anne, which gave it its name. Today several of north-east Brazil's main highways meet here, making it one of the region's busiest road junctions.
Q194343.w: A large, compact city on a flat plateau; highways radiating out in several directions; greener land east, drier scrub west.
f: It is the second-largest city in the state of Bahia.
Locals call it the 'Princess of the Sertão'.

q.q: What gave Feira de Santana its name?

Q2135.t: A prairie city on the bed of a vanished glacial lake
Q2135.s: Winnipeg sits on land so flat because it is the floor of an ancient lake: glacial Lake Agassiz, which covered much of this region at the end of the last ice age. The Red and Assiniboine rivers meet in the city centre, at a spot people have used as a meeting place for some 6,000 years. East of the city, look for a long, straight channel: the Red River Floodway.
Q2135.w: A city on dead-flat plains at a river junction; a long flood channel curving round its eastern side; square fields beyond.
f: The Floodway, about 47 km long, carries Red River floodwater around the city.
The name comes from a Cree word for 'muddy water', first given to Lake Winnipeg to the north.

q.q: What does the Cree word 'Winnipeg' mean?

Q744553.t: The polar bear town on the shore of Hudson Bay
Q744553.s: Churchill is a tiny town where the Churchill River meets Hudson Bay, right at the edge of the treeline: stunted spruce to the south, open tundra to the north. Every autumn polar bears gather along this coast, waiting for the bay to freeze so they can hunt seals on the ice. In summer thousands of beluga whales crowd into the river mouth.
Q744553.w: A small town on a rocky point at a river mouth on a huge grey bay; flat tundra and countless ponds inland.
f: No road reaches Churchill; it is linked to the south only by rail and by air.
Across the river mouth stands Prince of Wales Fort, a stone fort built by the Hudson's Bay Company between 1731 and 1771.

q.q: Why do polar bears gather near Churchill every autumn?
q.a: To wait for the bay to freeze
x: To find caves to hibernate in

Q2123.t: A capital planted by hand on the treeless prairie
Q2123.s: Regina rises from some of the flattest, most open prairie in Canada, where the only trees are the ones people planted. Before 1882 the spot was known as Pile o' Bones, after heaps of bison bones by the creek. That year Princess Louise renamed it Regina, Latin for 'queen', after her mother, Queen Victoria. Look for the man-made Wascana Lake in the city's green heart.
Q2123.w: A compact city on a vast, flat, chequered prairie; a curving lake and parkland in its centre; railway lines running straight out.
f: Wascana Centre, the park around the lake, is larger than New York's Central Park.
Canada's national police, the RCMP, has trained its recruits in Regina since the 1880s.

q.q: What was Regina's site called before 1882?

Q10566.t: The Bridge City on the South Saskatchewan River
Q10566.s: Saskatoon straddles the South Saskatchewan River, which winds through the city in a wooded valley crossed by a string of bridges — hence the nickname, the Bridge City. Around it, flat farmland stretches to the horizon in tidy squares of wheat and canola. The town was founded in 1883 as a temperance colony and named after a sweet local berry.
Q10566.w: A city on both banks of a winding river with several bridges close together; flat squares of cropland all around.
f: The saskatoon berry takes its name from the Cree word misâskwatômina.
Potash mines around the city tap one of the world's largest deposits of this fertiliser mineral.

q.q: What is Saskatoon named after?

Q36312.t: Where the prairie runs up against the Rockies
Q36312.s: Calgary sits where the flat prairie begins to ripple into foothills, and on a clear day the white wall of the Rocky Mountains fills the western horizon. The Bow and Elbow rivers meet downtown, where the North-West Mounted Police built Fort Calgary in 1875. In winter, look for a band of clear sky over the mountains: the chinook arch, sign of a warm wind.
Q36312.w: A large city on rolling land where plains meet foothills; two rivers joining in the centre; snowy mountains to the west.
f: A chinook wind can raise the temperature here by more than 20 °C in a few hours.
In 1988 Calgary hosted the first Winter Olympics held in Canada.

q.q: What is the warm winter wind that sweeps into Calgary called?
